title: Curcumin
summary: The main polyphenol of turmeric (Curcuma longa), studied for anti-inflammatory and anticancer properties. In a 2026 Wroclaw Medical University study comparing five natural compounds on fibrosarcoma cells, curcumin showed the most balanced profile: strong induction of cancer-cell senescence with a relatively favorable safety profile. Preclinical only — cell lines plus an insect model, not a treatment.

details.what_it_is: Curcumin is the main polyphenol of turmeric (Curcuma longa), widely studied for anti-inflammatory and anticancer properties.
details.evidence_level: preclinical (in vitro cell lines + greater wax moth larvae model)

study.title: Modulation of NFκB Signaling by Natural Compounds in Sarcoma and Normal Muscle Models
compounds_compared: CAPE (caffeic acid phenethyl ester, from propolis)

anticancer_research.mechanism_focus: Modulation of the NF-κB signaling pathway (inflammation, metabolism, cell survival, aging) — precise modulation, not complete suppression.
key_findings: All five compounds disrupted mitochondrial function: ATP fell ~83–92% in fibrosarcoma cells vs ~23–73% in healthy muscle cells, suggesting cancer cells are more vulnerable to energy-metabolism disruption.
All five induced cellular senescence in fibrosarcoma cells; curcumin was strongest, raising the senescent fraction from ~16.5% to more than 75%.

Curcumin and CAPE showed the greatest selectivity against fibrosarcoma cells; curcumin combined strong anticancer activity with a relatively favorable safety profile — the most balanced profile of the five compounds.
In the wax moth larva toxicity model, berberine and curcumin were best tolerated; CAPE and cucurbitacin E caused higher mortality; biochanin A was the most toxic.
anticancer_research.limitations: In vitro cell lines plus an invertebrate model only — the authors explicitly state this does not mean curcumin can be used to treat sarcomas. Next steps: advanced in vivo models, mechanism, optimal dosing and delivery.
